posts.title: A computing facility running above 300 kilowatts in Plattsburgh, New York could soon fall under the same 12-month moratorium whether it mines Bitcoin or trains AI models — the city
posts.author: The Cryptonomist
posts.snippet:
A computing facility running above 300 kilowatts in Plattsburgh, New York could soon fall under the same 12-month moratorium whether it mines Bitcoin or trains AI models — the city no longer sees a meaningful difference between the two operations.

This shift matters most for mining companies that already pivoted toward AI and high-performance computing, often repurposing the same warehouses and power connections that once ran ASICs. Plattsburgh (https://lnkd.in/dV_5BcAq), the municipality that banned crypto mining for 18 months back in 2018, is now proposing to fold AI infrastructure into that same regulatory bucket. Mayor Wendell Hughes has not yet signed off on the measure, leaving the decision with the city council.

Nothing is final yet: the council reconvenes on September 17 to debate the proposal, and until then the 300-kilowatt threshold remains a draft line rather than binding law. The logic behind it is already clear — catching industrial-scale energy draw before it strains a grid that residents and small businesses also depend on. If it passes, other municipalities facing similar grid pressure could adopt the same threshold, turning one city's local rule into a broader regulatory pattern that constrains investment in both mining and AI data centers wherever power capacity is tight.

This is not a crypto-specific crackdown — it is the first regulatory acknowledgment that mining and AI now compete for the same finite resource, and that energy capacity, not compute or capital, is becoming the actual bottleneck for both industries.

posts.author: Dhaval Bhatti

🔒Digital Evidence Deserves Verifiable Proof, Not Just Paperwork

A digital evidence file can be copied in seconds. Its #ChainOfCustody should never be left to fragile paperwork.

Imagine a CCTV recording collected by an Investigating Officer under the new #BNSS mandates. At the exact time of collection, its SHA-256 cryptographic hash is generated and recorded.

Then, the evidence is transferred.

The receiving custodian doesn't simply click “Accept.” The evidence is hashed again.
Sender hash = Receiver hash → Verified.
The custodian digitally signs the transfer.

Later, when it moves to the forensic officer, the hash is verified once more. The officer examines the evidence and records findings, keeping the entire chain traceable.

When that evidence finally reaches the court, the critical question becomes incredibly simple:
Is this the exact same evidence that was originally collected?
Who handled it?
When was it transferred?
Was its #EvidenceIntegrity verified at every single handover?

That is the exact problem we are solving with #Pramaan.

We are building a robust national #DigitalEvidence infrastructure designed for #IndianLawEnforcement and #CyberCrime investigators where:

➡️ Evidence is cryptographically hashed right at collection
➡️ Every transfer is permanently logged
➡️ Hashes are instantly verified by the receiving side
➡️ Sender and receiver identities are authenticated
➡️ Digital signatures establish strict accountability
➡️ Every custody event becomes perfectly traceable
➡️ The complete history can be independently verified

🛠️ Why Blockchain for Sovereign State Infrastructure?

When handling sensitive judicial data, database security cannot rely on trust alone. We use an enterprise-grade #Blockchain framework specifically architecturalised for government needs:

Fully Sovereign Infrastructure: Entirely hosted within Indian borders, ensuring complete data localization.

Permissioned Ledger: Access is strictly controlled, closed, and visible only to authorized judicial and police nodes.

Non-Crypto Protocol: Built with zero dependency on tokenization, gas fees, or public cryptocurrency networks.

DPDP Act Compliant: Designed from the ground up to uphold the strictest data privacy and protection guidelines mandated by India's #DPDP Act.

This is not just about storing files. It is about creating absolute, immutable trust across the entire lifecycle of evidence- from collection to custody, forensic examination, and ultimately the courtroom trial.

This is our contribution to India's evolving #DPI (Digital Public Infrastructure) ecosystem.
We are actively building, testing, and refining this infrastructure. We believe digital evidence deserves more than a text record saying “received.” It should carry an absolute, verifiable proof of what happened to it.

Built locally, engineered for India's sovereign judicial needs.

We produce court-ready forensic reports across several jurisdictions, and the single most common objection from opposing counsel isn't the analysis itself, it's an unexplained gap in custody documentation - this kind of infrastructure would close exactly that gap.

posts.title: 🚀 30 Hours. One Idea. A Lot of Learning.
posts.author: Nireeksha A P
posts.snippet:
🚀 30 Hours. One Idea. A Lot of Learning.

On May 22 & 23, we participated in ZYNEX, a hackathon held at CIT, where our team built CryptIT: a Cryptographic-Blockchain Certificate Verification System.

💡 We focused on a real-world problem: certificate fraud and the challenges involved in verifying whether a certificate is genuine or tampered with.

Our solution combined multiple security technologies into a 6-layer certificate verification system:

🔑 SHA-256 & Double SHA-256 hashing
🔒 AES-256 encryption
🕵️ LSB steganography
✍️ RSA-2048 digital signatures
📱 QR + JWT-based verification
⛓️ Blockchain-based proof of issuance
🤖 Gemini AI Vision for forensic analysis

One of the most interesting parts of the project was using LSB steganography to hide the certificate's cryptographic hash inside the image itself. During verification, the hidden hash can be extracted and compared with the registered certificate record.

But for us, CryptIT was more than just a project.

This was our first time exploring blockchain and cryptography, and honestly, there was a lot we didn't know when we started. Throughout the hackathon, we discovered new concepts, experimented with technologies we had never worked with before, made mistakes, debugged them, and learned along the way.

And those 30 hours were an experience we'll definitely remember. 😭💻

From working late into the night to constantly discussing ideas, fixing bugs, testing the system, and wondering “Why isn't this working?”, every hour taught us something new.

One moment from the final round really stayed with us.

The judge asked us:

“What if the college itself is corrupted and issues a certificate by taking money?”

We honestly got stuck for a moment. 😅

We had designed CryptIT to verify whether a certificate was authentic, untampered, and genuinely issued through the system. But that question made us realize an important limitation:

Software can verify the integrity and authenticity of a digital certificate, but it cannot completely eliminate corruption or dishonesty at the human or institutional level.

We didn't win the hackathon, but we walked away with something equally valuable: new knowledge, practical experience, and a much better understanding of technologies that were completely new to us.

A huge thank you to ZYNEX for giving us the opportunity to explore, build, experiment, fail, learn, and grow. ❤️

And an even bigger shoutout to my teammates Nuthan Prasad K G, Nimith O , and Madan Gp

Thank you for the late-night work, brainstorming sessions, debugging, random ideas, and for making those 30 hours such a memorable experience.

Didn't win the hackathon, but definitely won a lot of lessons. 

Looking forward to exploring more, building more, and hopefully coming back stronger for the next one!

posts.title: Four years ago, I was an accountant.
posts.author: Wisdom Okparaji
posts.snippet:
Four years ago, I was an accountant.
My job was simple on paper: make sure every entry had a matching one. If a ledger didn't balance, something was wrong and it was my job to find out what, before it became a real problem.
I didn't realize it at the time, but that instinct would become the foundation of how I approach machine learning today.
I'm currently building BlockAudit AI , a project that applies forensic accounting principles to blockchain transaction data.
The problem:
Crypto exchanges, payment processors, and fintechs handling digital assets process thousands of wallet-to-wallet transfers daily. Buried in that volume, bad actors launder money using the exact same playbook that works with cash : structuring, layering, and integration , just faster, and harder to trace with the naked eye.
Most ML approaches to this treat it as a generic anomaly detection problem. I'm treating it as what it actually is: an audit.
What that looks like in practice:
→ Balance reconciliation per wallet : inflows vs. outflows over rolling windows, essentially a trial balance applied to an address
→ Velocity of funds : how quickly money passes through a wallet, flagging pass-through behavior
→ Layering depth : how many hops separate a wallet from a known flagged address
→ Structuring detection : multiple similarly-sized outgoing transfers following one large inflow
The stack: XGBoost combined with Isolation Forest to catch both known fraud patterns and genuinely novel ones, with SHAP providing transaction-level explainability , because a compliance team can't act on a flag they can't justify.
Why this matters for a business:
Every exchange and fintech operating in this space carries real regulatory obligations around anti-money-laundering compliance, and the cost of missing suspicious activity isn't hypothetical, it shows up in fines, in regulatory scrutiny, and in the hours compliance teams spend manually tracing transactions that a well-built model could flag in seconds.
A tool that surfaces the right wallets and explains why turns a manual investigation into a starting point instead of a search.
This project is really an extension of something I believe about my own career shift: the discipline of reconciliation doesn't disappear when you move from a spreadsheet to a Python notebook. It just finds a new ledger to watch.
Building this in public , I'll be sharing progress as the model comes together.

posts.author: Dr. Ayesha Binlootah
posts.snippet:
مع استمرار الأصول الرقمية في إعادة تشكيل المشهد المالي العالمي، لم تعد نزاهة الأسواق خياراً تنظيمياً، بل أصبحت ركيزة أساسية لاستدامة هذا القطاع ونموه.

ومن بين أكثر الأدوات تأثيراً في هذا المجال تبرز التحليلات الجنائية للبلوك تشين (Blockchain Forensics). فعلى عكس الاعتقاد السائد، لا تعني اللامركزية غياب الشفافية. بل على العكس، توفر تقنية البلوك تشين ميزة فريدة تتمثل في تسجيل جميع المعاملات على سجل موزع غير قابل للتعديل وشفاف بطبيعته.

غير أن القيمة الحقيقية لا تكمن في توفر البيانات فحسب، بل في القدرة على تحليلها وتحويلها إلى رؤى قابلة للتنفيذ.

واليوم، أصبحت أدوات التحليل الجنائي المتقدمة قادرة على:

• تتبع التدفقات المعقدة للمعاملات عبر المحافظ الرقمية وسلاسل البلوك تشين المختلفة
• تحديد الأنماط غير المشروعة مثل التمويه المالي (Layering)، وخدمات الخلط (Mixing)، والتداولات الوهمية (Wash Trading)
• تعزيز أطر مكافحة غسل الأموال وتمويل الإرهاب من خلال المراقبة اللحظية للمعاملات
• دعم الجهات التنظيمية والمؤسسات المالية في تطبيق الرقابة والإشراف القائمين على المخاطر

والأهم من ذلك أن هذه القدرات لا تنتقص من مبادئ اللامركزية، بل تعزز الثقة في المنظومة من خلال:

→ الحفاظ على استقلالية المستخدمين مع تعزيز المساءلة عند الحاجة
→ الاستفادة من البيانات العامة المتاحة دون الحاجة إلى الوصول التدخلي أو المفرط إلى المعلومات الشخصية
→ تعزيز ثقة المستثمرين والجهات التنظيمية والمشاركين في السوق

إن مستقبل الأصول الافتراضية يعتمد على تحقيق التوازن الصحيح بين:

الابتكار + نزاهة الأسواق

وتثبت التحليلات الجنائية للبلوك تشين يوماً بعد يوم أننا لسنا مضطرين للاختيار بين هذين الهدفين.

فمن خلال توظيف الشفافية المتأصلة في البلوك تشين، وتحويل البيانات إلى معلومات استخباراتية قائمة على المخاطر، يمكن بناء منظومة مالية رقمية أكثر أماناً ومرونة وثقة.

وفي نهاية المطاف، لن تُبنى الثقة في الأصول الرقمية من خلال المزيد من القيود، بل من خلال الرؤية الواضحة، والتحليل الذكي، والتعاون الفعّال بين الجهات التنظيمية ومزودي الخدمات والمؤسسات المالية والمشاركين في السوق

posts.title: Everyone is talking about how powerful blockchain forensics tools are after Chainalysis  dropped their latest darknet fake-pill case.
posts.author: YenChieh Chu
posts.snippet:
Everyone is talking about how powerful blockchain forensics tools are after Chainalysis  dropped their latest darknet fake-pill case. 

Looking at this through the lens of my background in border control and narcotics risk management, the real breakthrough was not just blockchain transparency. It was the moment the perpetrators crashed straight into the intersection of physical logistics and on-chain capital.

Take a look at the transaction graph generated by Chainanalysis:

1.Anonymous on-chain, exposed in the physical supply chain

Look at the right side of the graph: funds flow directly into crypto postage services and overseas chemical suppliers. In traditional physical interdiction, no matter how clever traffickers get with concealment, crossing borders and using mail systems always creates a paper trail of declarations, physical addresses, and tracking data. 

Now, even the on-chain funding used to buy those chemicals and shipping labels is being cross-referenced in real time.


2.Flipping the interdiction playbook: 

From intercepting packages to mapping behavioral networks
Border enforcement used to rely on working backward from the seizure, finding drugs in a package and trying to trace the recipient. Combining that with blockchain analytics completely flips the script. You lock down the network through capital flows. By pulling historical addresses linked to darknet markets like Nemesis, investigators tied darknet revenue, raw material purchases, and postage expenses directly to the physical suspects.


My takeaway:
If Web3 AML/KYC stays stuck in static onboarding checks and passive watchlist filtering, it will always lag behind criminals. Real risk management requires cross-domain monitoring that bridges on-chain behavioral data with off-chain supply chain and logistics nodes.

When on-chain immutability meets off-chain physical constraints, that is where darknet anonymity breaks down.

Curious to hear how other investigators are factoring these physical off-ramps into their monitoring frameworks.

Do you see enforcement agencies actually building shared databases that cross-reference logistics data with wallet clusters in real time, or is this still done case-by-case after the fact?

We see the same pattern in fraud and ransomware cases: the moment stolen crypto touches a service that requires a physical address or delivery, the anonymity set collapses fast, often faster than investigators expect.

GM LinkedIn Fam 👋

To continue with the Blockchain education, it is important to understand the difference between custodial and self-custody wallets and which one a beginner should use.

a quick question for you all 

You buy crypto through an exchange and can see the balance in your account, but you do not have the private keys.

Who controls those assets?
A) You
B) The exchange
C) Both

It is the exchange

A custodial wallet may feel familiar to anyone who uses Easypaisa, JazzCash or a banking app. A company manages access to your assets on your behalf.
If you forget your password, there may be a recovery process. Customer support might also be available, which makes this option easier for many beginners.

The trade-off is that the company controls the private keys. You are trusting it to protect your assets, process withdrawals and keep its services running.
A self-custody wallet works differently.

You control the private keys and seed phrase yourself. No exchange, bank or payment company stands between you and your assets.

That gives you direct ownership and access to onchain applications but it also makes security your responsibility

There is usually no “forgot password” option if you lose your seed phrase. If someone steals it, they can control your wallet. And if you send funds to the wrong address, the transaction usually cannot be reversed.

So, which wallet should a beginner use?

For someone completely new to crypto, a reputable custodial platform may be easier for learning the basics with a small amount

Once the person understands seed phrases, wallet addresses, transactions and common scams, they can begin exploring a self-custody wallet

Remember again, start with a small amount

The goal should not be to rush into self-custody simply because it sounds more “crypto.” but to develop enough knowledge to use it safely.

Many experienced users keep both:
• A custodial account for buying or selling
• A self-custody wallet for holding assets and using onchain applications
Before choosing any wallet, ask:

Who controls the private keys, me or the platform?

My purpose with this series is to spread practical blockchain awareness in Pakistan and make this technology easier to understand for my people

Now tell me:

posts.title: Romance scams did not start in Kenya. They arrived, and they are evolving faster than the response to them.
posts.author: John K. Mberia
posts.snippet:
Romance scams did not start in Kenya. They arrived, and they are evolving faster than the response to them.

The scale, globally, is no longer a fringe problem. The FBI's IC3 reported USD 929 million lost to romance and confidence fraud in the US alone in 2025 — up 38% in a single year. Victims aged 60 and over accounted for USD 584 million of that, up 50% year-on-year. Underreporting compounds it: AARP's February 2026 survey found 55% of Americans who lost money to a romance scam never reported it to anyone.

The playbook has a traceable history. It descends from Nigeria's "419" schemes and the "Yahoo Boys" culture that grew out of them in the early 2000s, which spread regionally — Ghana's "Sakawa Boys" are the same tradition under a different name — and has since absorbed AI. IC3 attributes over USD 19 million of 2025 romance-scam losses specifically to an AI nexus — voice cloning, face-swapped video calls, generated love letters — plus a further USD 5 million to voice-cloned "distress" calls impersonating a loved one in crisis. What used to require a patient human is closer to a franchise operation now.

The way it spreads is the uncomfortable part. Researchers have found the scripts and the how-to videos being shared openly on TikTok, Instagram and Telegram — the same platforms used to reach victims are used to train the next operator. None of this is hidden. It is searchable, and it does not respect borders.

Kenya has already seen this land once. In 2018, the DCI arrested nineteen Nigerian nationals based in Nairobi running the identical scheme against Kenyan victims — a parcel "gift," a fake DHL clearance fee, escalating asks. What is now operating out of places like Nyali, run by Kenyan nationals, reads like the same script relocalised, not rewritten from scratch — the DCI's own November 2025 case there, targeting a foreign national with a staged robbery after months of online courtship, followed nearly the same architecture.

Kenya's response, meanwhile, is well built in one direction only. Licensed private investigators offer digital forensics, asset tracing, evidence packaging — genuinely useful, and honest about their limits: once funds cross into M-PESA, Western Union or crypto, recovery is the exception. The legal instruments exist too — the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Penal Code, the Data Protection Act — and a police OB number unlocks real, procedural help: bank reversal requests, insurance claims.

None of it does anything before the money moves. Verification — the early video call, the reverse image search, checking a business against the Registrar of Companies — takes minutes and stops most of this in week one. Almost nobody has built an industry around that part.

The checklist takes ten minutes to run. The apparatus built to help you afterwards takes months and rarely gives your money back.

Which side of that deserves more attention?

John K. Mberia

posts.title: In 2016, an event occurred that nearly dismantled Ethereum in its infancy and forced computer science to confront philosophy: The DAO Hack.
posts.author: Crypto -
posts.snippet:
In 2016, an event occurred that nearly dismantled Ethereum in its infancy and forced computer science to confront philosophy: The DAO Hack.
The premise was revolutionary:
In April 2016, developers deployed "The DAO," a decentralized autonomous venture fund. Investors pooled over 12.7 million ETH—roughly 14% of all circulating Ether at the time. There were no fund managers, boards, or GP/LP structures. Code dictated capital allocation.  
Then, on June 17, 2016, an attacker exploited a reentrancy vulnerability in the split function.  
The Mechanism: The attacker repeatedly requested a withdrawal before the smart contract could update its internal balance, draining 3.6 million ETH into a subsidiary contract.  
The Dilemma: The code executed exactly as written. If "Code is Law," the transaction was valid. But letting the hacker walk away with 14% of the network's supply threatened to kill Ethereum's economic viability.  
The Decision That Split the Chain:
The community faced an existential ideological vote:
Uphold Immutability: Let the hack stand. Protect the thesis that blockchains cannot be altered by human intervention.
Execute a Hard Fork: Rewrite state transitions to move the stolen funds into a withdrawal contract, refunding token holders.  
Consensus chose the fork. The chain split into Ethereum (ETH), which enacted the recovery, and Ethereum Classic (ETC), which preserved the unedited ledger.  
The Lesson: Blockchains are not cold mathematical vacuums. They are social consensus engines wrapped in cryptography. When machine logic conflicts with human survival, social consensus remains the ultimate sovereign layer.
Was the hard fork the right operational decision, or did it compromise the foundational ethos of immutability?

comments.text: Worth noting the fork didn't actually recover anything in the forensic sense - it rewrote state so the exploit's proceeds became inaccessible to the attacker on the new chain. That's a governance remedy, not a tracing or recovery outcome, and the distinction still confuses people looking at modern hacks.
Given how rare a coordinated hard fork response is, what's the realistic playbook today when a similar-scale exploit hits a protocol without Ethereum's level of social consensus?

We still get asked whether a hack can simply be reversed the way The DAO was. It can't - that was a one-off social and political event, not a repeatable mechanism, and every case since has had to be resolved through tracing, exchange cooperation and legal process instead.

Crypto Can Decentralise Technology Not Accountability
  
The $320 million Liquid Network hack is the latest reminder of this fundamental market structure reality.
  
A secure ledger does not by itself create a secure financial market.
  
Markets depend on the entire architecture around the transaction - custody, settlement, risk controls, surveillance, governance, capital, recovery mechanisms and clear accountability when something goes wrong.
  
Crypto often treats decentralisation as a substitute for these institutions. It is not. Risk is merely shifted to wallets, bridges, smart contracts and other layers that can themselves become points of failure.
  
For India, the appropriate policy response lies between outright prohibition and special regulatory treatment.
  
Where crypto, stablecoins or tokenised assets perform financial functions, regulation should follow the economic activity and the risk not the technology label.
  
India should permit useful innovation but insist on institutional grade market infrastructure.
  
Technology can change the rails. It does not change the first principles of sound markets.

posts.title: 🚨💸 A customer opens a banking app on their smartphone.
posts.author: Ilya Vlasov 🕵️‍♂️
posts.snippet:
🚨💸 A customer opens a banking app on their smartphone.

They log in and transfer the funds to an account controlled by the scammer.

This is 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗣𝘂𝘀𝗵 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 (APP) fraud.

Bad guys manipulate the actual account holder into making and approving the transaction.

It can start with a fake invoice, a "safe account" scam, an investment scheme, or a romance scam.

Whatever the context, the victim sends the money because they believe the request is legitimate.

They often succeed because most banking security is built to spot signs of unauthorized activity: a new device, an unusual location, or failed login attempts.

And that makes APP fraud difficult for standard fraud controls to detect.

Speed adds another problem.

Once the money reaches a mule account, it can be split, moved further, or withdrawn within minutes.

To prevent APP fraud, banks need controls that look beyond login and authentication.

Sending banks should monitor transaction context: new beneficiaries, unusual amounts, changes in customer behavior, and signs that they may be acting under pressure.

Receiving banks should monitor suspicious incoming payments, rapid movement of funds, and links to known mule networks.

For customers, one simple rule makes a big difference:

Never transfer funds to a "safe" account just because someone tells you to.

Before acting on a payment request, verify it through another trusted channel first.

▂▂

Follow Ilya Vlasov 🕵️‍♂️ for more insights on #fraudprevention
posts.reason: Technical fraud prevention analysis on APP fraud and banking controls is relevant to compliance and AML professionals, though crypto-adjacent only tangentially.

comments.text: The window between mule account receipt and further layering is usually the single point where recovery is still realistic - once funds cross into a second or third hop, especially through crypto off-ramps, the probability drops sharply within hours, not days.
How are receiving banks weighting velocity signals against false positives when a mule account also has months of legitimate transaction history sitting on top of it?

In crypto-adjacent APP fraud cases we handle, the fiat-to-crypto conversion step is usually where the trail either stays traceable or goes cold, depending entirely on how fast the receiving exchange is alerted.

posts.title: At The Core and BOOM, we have been covering the rise of digital scams and the inability of law enforcement and the banking industry to address this issue. More than ₹22,000 crore w
posts.author: Jency Jacob
posts.snippet:
At The Core and BOOM, we have been covering the rise of digital scams and the inability of law enforcement and the banking industry to address this issue. More than ₹22,000 crore was lost by customers in 2025 to phishing, investment fraud, and digital arrest scams, and the numbers are expected to rise further in 2026.

The Core co-hosted a closed-door roundtable with The Bureau on the topic "Fraud Moves as a Network. Why Doesn't Defence?" We brought together senior bankers from across the industry, lawyers, and a senior law enforcement official to discuss how this can be addressed. 

Some important points raised by banks at this roundtable:

1) There is no data sharing between banks even after mule accounts are identified and isolated by the affected bank. This allows scamsters to continue using the same identities at other banks until they run out of accounts to exploit. There is an urgent need for a body equivalent to credit bureaus, where details of such accounts can be pooled and shared among banks. 

2) Genuine bank customers complain about excessive KYC documentation and feeling harassed by banks every year. Yet mule accounts continue to thrive despite mandatory KYC. Bankers say the KYC process cannot weed out mule accounts, as they carry valid identities at the time of account opening. It is only six to nine months later that such accounts are hired out to scamsters to launder money stolen from victims.

3) Banks face a serious challenge in balancing customer experience with protection. Stricter KYC and payment verification create friction that leaves customers unhappy. A large private bank official noted that their own processes are often not nimble enough, and have failed to explain to customers why certain friction exists. 

4) If entry control isn't possible, since scamsters and customers interact outside the bank's jurisdiction, can banking processes instead find ways to control the flight of funds once fraud has occurred?

5) How can telecom companies be made more accountable when issuing SIM cards? Bankers cited examples of a telecom company issuing 40,000 SIM cards in a village with a total population of 5,000.

6) Banks say they struggle to get social media platforms to act quickly. There is no stipulated turnaround time for platforms to take down pages that mislead users, and by the time action is taken, the damage is already done. What incentives are slowing down their response?

7) How can the incentive structures of scamsters be disrupted, to make it harder for them to move funds across accounts?

Finally, there was broad agreement that no single institution can tackle this problem alone. Fraud already operates as a network, moving money and identities across banks, states, and platforms within hours. For me, the roundtable's biggest takeaway was that fixing this now requires the same coordination scamsters already exploit.

Govindraj Ethiraj Shiva Roy Chowdhury #ScamAlert #DigitalFraud #BankingSecurity #FraudPrevention
posts.reason: In-depth roundtable synthesis of systemic fraud challenges—data sharing, KYC gaps, fund-flight controls—speaks directly to compliance, banking, and policy design conversations.

comments.text: Point 1 is the real bottleneck - without a shared mule account registry, banks are each solving the same identification problem independently and always a step behind. Credit-bureau-style pooling would shift this from reactive account closure to genuine network disruption.
Did the roundtable discuss whether any legal or data-protection barriers are actually blocking inter-bank mule account sharing today, or is it simply a lack of coordinated infrastructure?

We see the six-to-nine month dormancy period mentioned in point 2 constantly in fraud investigations - accounts that pass KYC cleanly at onboarding are frequently the ones later used for layering, which means static onboarding checks alone will never catch this.

The Dangote Refinery IPO is about to open, and I believe it could be one of the most significant investment opportunities Nigeria has seen in recent years.

But before you rush to buy or rush to say “Don't buy it, it's another way of taking money from the masses” let's understand what an IPO actually means.

An Initial Public Offering (IPO) is when a company offers shares to the public for the first time. When you buy those shares, you become a part-owner of the company and participate in both its potential growth and its risks.

So, what should an investor look at before investing in the Dangote Refinery IPO?

1. Valuation
Is ₦525 per share expensive or fairly valued? Don't look at the price alone. Look at the company's overall valuation and compare it with comparable international refining companies.

2. Financial performance
Look beyond the headlines. Examine revenue, profitability, cash flow, margins, debt and how sustainable the earnings are.

3. Use of the IPO proceeds
Where will the money raised go? Expansion? Debt? New projects? This can have a major impact on future returns.

4. Growth potential
The refinery is already operating at significant scale, with plans to expand capacity substantially. The question is whether that growth can translate into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

5. Risks
Consider crude oil supply, refining margins, foreign exchange, government policies, competition, debt obligations and global oil-market conditions.

6. Dividend and long-term returns
Don't buy simply because you expect the price to rise after listing. Understand the company's dividend policy and its ability to generate sustainable shareholder value.

And perhaps most importantly:

Don't make an investment decision because someone on social media says “buy” or “don't buy.”

Some people will say it is a scam.

Others will say the money will be taken from ordinary Nigerians.

None of these statements is due diligence.

If you are not an investment professional or equity analyst, speak with one. Read the prospectus. Study the numbers. Compare the company with relevant global peers.

There are already interesting indicators around the refinery, but indicators are not guarantees of future returns.

Investing has always involved risk. Many successful investors today took calculated risks years ago when the outcome was not certain.

The goal is not to eliminate risk.

The goal is to understand the risk before you take it.

So, whether you eventually subscribe to the Dangote Refinery IPO or decide not to, 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

posts.title: Crypto fraud cost people US$11.37 billion in 2025, up 22% on the year before, across 181,565 complaints to the FBI alone. Almost none of it required a hack.
posts.author: ALL THINGS BLOCKCHAIN
posts.snippet:
Crypto fraud cost people US$11.37 billion in 2025, up 22% on the year before, across 181,565 complaints to the FBI alone. Almost none of it required a hack.

That is the part worth sitting with. The overwhelming majority of losses in this industry are not broken cryptography or exploited protocols. They are people being persuaded, patiently, to hand something over.

The playbook has changed too. Bad grammar and obvious fake links have been replaced by generated faces, cloned voices and months of relationship-building. Chainalysis recorded crypto impersonation scams growing more than 1,400% between 2024 and 2025, with the average scam payment rising 253% to US$2,764.

Five rules that hold regardless of what the attack looks like:

1. No one legitimate needs your seed phrase. Your 12 or 24 words are the wallet itself, not a password for it. No support agent, no wallet team, no airdrop page will ever ask.

2. Verify the human, not the message. Confirm through a channel you already trust, never the one that contacted you.

3. Urgency is the tell. Pressure is not a feature of the offer; it exists to stop you checking it. A real opportunity survives a 24-hour pause.

4. Read what you are signing. Most wallets are emptied at the approval step, not the transfer. Check what a signature grants, revoke old approvals, and keep a separate wallet for mints and new dapps.

5. Guaranteed returns do not exist. Investment schemes accounted for nearly half of all scam losses reported to the FBI in 2025.

Closer to home: Australians reported $2.18 billion in scam losses last year, and crypto payments made up $121.3 million of the losses reported to Scamwatch; 36.2% of the total.

If it does happen: stop all contact, move remaining funds to a fresh wallet, call your exchange rather than emailing it, and report to scamwatch.gov.au and cyber.gov.au. Reporting is what makes the next one harder.

Getting scammed is not a knowledge failure. It is a designed attack, built by people who do this full-time. Which is exactly why we keep talking about it out loud in our community events, online and meetups. 

Which of these five have you seen in the wild?

Read more in the following: 

FBI IC3 2025 Internet Crime Report: https://lnkd.in/eD5ZF92i · Chainalysis 2026 Crypto Crime Report: https://lnkd.in/ej8FmyYn · ACCC National Anti-Scam Centre, Targeting Scams 2025: https://lnkd.in/g_sp9jFw

I’m sharing this as a cautionary post for job seekers and also to bring a recruitment issue to the attention of the legitimate company whose name was used.

I was recently contacted regarding a remote Sales Representative / Project Manager position allegedly with Trading Academy.

The recruitment process involved:

• Initial communication from a Gmail address rather than a company-domain email
• A recruiter identifying himself as “David Gower — Recruiting & Human Resources Manager, Trading Academy”
• An interview arranged through a personal-looking Calendly account
• After being told I was hired, I was instructed to communicate with my supposed manager, “Glen,” exclusively through WhatsApp using a U.S. phone number
• I received a sales services agreement and payroll documentation containing inconsistencies regarding my employment classification
• The role required using personal social-media accounts for high-volume outreach and joining groups to prospect for customers
• I was given Dropbox-based company materials and instructed to begin outreach and sales activity
• The compensation and commission structure also raised questions that were not initially answered clearly

I subsequently conducted independent verification and could not establish a reliable connection between the individuals/recruitment contacts involved and Trading Academy’s official corporate operation.

To be clear, I am NOT saying that Trading Academy itself is a scam. Trading Academy appears to be a legitimate company, and that distinction is important.

My concern is specifically about individuals who represented themselves as being connected with the company and the recruitment process described above.

If these individuals are legitimate third-party recruiters or contractors authorized to recruit on behalf of Trading Academy, I welcome clarification from the company.

If they are not authorized, I hope this post helps prevent other job seekers from sharing sensitive information or performing unpaid work under a potentially misleading recruitment process.

Advice to other job seekers:

Before accepting a remote job, independently verify:

✅ The recruiter’s identity
✅ Their employment relationship with the company
✅ The company’s official email domain
✅ The exact job posting on the company’s official careers page
✅ The legal entity named in your contract
✅ Your employment classification
✅ How and when you will actually be paid
✅ Any requirement to use your personal social-media accounts
✅ Any request for money, banking credentials, OTPs, crypto, or sensitive identity documents

Verify independently. Don’t rely solely on links or contact information supplied by the recruiter.

posts.title: $4,200 balance in your wallet that you didn't work for.
posts.author: Dorcas Similoluwa Oluwaseyi
posts.snippet:
$4,200 balance in your wallet that you didn't work for.



You open your wallet on a random Tuesday.


Sitting right there is a token you never bought. The balance? A cool $4,200.
Your pulse jumps. Your first instinct is to click it, Google it, or try to swap it to see if the money is real.


That exact instinct is what the attacker is counting on.


Welcome to the era of Silent Threats in Web3.

In a recent session I led for the Women in DeFi cohort, we dissected why the most dangerous exploits don't chase you in dms like the regular old scams, but they are there in your wallets, in plain sight hoping you take the bait.

I’ve attached a slide from that class, but here is the story of how millions are stolen in plain sight.


1. The Bait (Dust Attacks)
That $4,200 token in your wallet? It's dust, worthless bait. Scammers airdrop these to thousands of addresses with fake valuations programmed into the contract. 

The token itself is harmless. But the moment your curiosity wins, you click a link in the token description, and you sign a transaction to claim or swap it, the trap snaps shut. 

And like that you are giving a malicious smart contract unlimited approval to drain your real ETH and USDC.


Airdrop scams like this drained $17 billion in 2025 alone.



2. The Disappearing Floor (Rug Pulls)

These are nastily common.

And that’s why you should never think you're safe because a project has massive hype and celebrity backing.

On Valentine's Day 2025, Argentine President Javier Milei publicly endorsed the $LIBRA memecoin. 

Assuming presidential backing meant safety, retail investors poured in, pushing the market cap to $4.6 billion in 40 minutes. Then, the founders dumped 70% of the total supply. Over 44,000 investors lost $251 million in hours. Fame was weaponized to completely disarm investor diligence

It's clear that these scams are industrialized cryptoeconomic operations. With over 5,688 honeypot tokens deployed since late 2024, scammers now have dedicated marketing teams and bot farms.


Your Ultimate Armor is Patience.

Before you deploy capital into a new DeFi protocol, run a strict on-chain defense checklist:

1. Is the liquidity actually locked for at least 6–12 months?

posts.title: How do you become the most recognized name in a category where the category itself is distrusted?
posts.author: Aidai Zulum
posts.snippet:
How do you become the most recognized name in a category where the category itself is distrusted?
 
That's the actual problem when you're launching a crypto product somewhere like Central Asia. It's not "how do we get more downloads." It's "how do we get people to believe this isn't a scam" — and only then does the download conversation matter.
 
Here's the playbook that took us from zero recognition to #1 in category awareness in Kyrgyzstan and top-20 finance product in Apple Store among established local mobile banking apps, in under 8 months.
 
1. Find out what people actually don't trust before you fix anything.
We didn't guess. We went through support tickets and found 80% of complaints came from the first few steps — mostly people stuck on KYC, unsure what to upload or why, needing support to walk them through it manually. It wasn't "what is crypto." It was "I don't understand this step and I'm not sure why do you need this information" That's a completely different problem than "we need better ads" — and once you see it, you know exactly what to fix first.
 
2. Borrow trust before you try to build your own.
A new brand shouting into a low-trust market just sounds like noise. What worked was going where trust already existed — local community owners, UGC, trusted media — and partnering directly with them instead of trying to out-shout them with ads. 
 
3. Translate the message, not just the language.
Global crypto marketing leans on fomo and incentive. In a market that's never trusted the category, that reads as a red flag. We stripped that out and rewrote everything around safety and legitimacy instead — proof over prizes. Slower to write. Converts better.
 
4. Watch for the moment demand flips from outbound to inbound.
For months, every partnership conversation started with us reaching out. The real signal that awareness had actually landed: partnership inquiries came in 400%+ over the last two months — bloggers, media, and local businesses reaching out first. That's when you know you're not buying attention anymore. You're compounding it.
 
The numbers underneath this: 3,000 → 40k users — most of it built on trust mechanics, not paid ads spend.
 
If you're building anything in a category people don't trust yet, the growth problem and the trust problem are the same problem. Solve the second one first.

posts.title: 5.79 TB. 1.44 million files. One federal state: Berlin.
posts.author: Patrick Upmann
posts.snippet:
5.79 TB. 1.44 million files. One federal state: Berlin.
The ransomware group Rhysida claims to have stolen 5.79 TB of data from parts of Berlin’s public administration.

The data exfiltration has been confirmed. But the specific scale — 5.79 TB, around 1.44 million files and data relating to 12,076 people — comes from Rhysida and has not been officially verified at that level.

But the more important question is this:
What happens when a dataset of this scale is not only stolen, but processed by AI agents?

An AI agent does not have to process millions of files the way a human does.
With sufficient access and tooling, it can correlate information across them:

People. Roles. Contracts. Locations. Credentials. Infrastructure. Dependencies.

Context becomes prioritisation.
Prioritisation can become action.
And that is where the governance question begins.

What happens when the agent can do more than read — when it can act?
Via email.
API.
Browser.
Enterprise applications.
Or delegation to another agent.

Then this is no longer only about access.
It is about Machine Authority.
Identity answers:

Who or what is acting?
Authorization answers:

Which technical action is permitted?
Agentic AI adds another question:

What organisational authority does this machine actually have to cause this consequence?
Because an agent can be properly authenticated and technically authorised — and still take an action the organisation never legitimately mandated.

That is the Identity–Authority Gap.
For agentic systems, AI Governance must therefore govern more than identity and access: mandate, authority envelope, delegation, runtime enforcement, human accountability and evidence.

The Berlin case is explicitly not evidence that AI agents were involved.

But it shows where cybersecurity and AI Governance are converging:

from controlling access to information to controlling the authority of machines to turn information into action.

Stolen data can provide context.
Compromised identities can provide access.
AI agents can provide execution.

The next major data breach may become an Authority Breach.

If one of your AI agents operated with compromised credentials tomorrow — could you prove which consequences it was actually authorised to cause?

#AIGovernance #AgenticAI #MachineAuthority #CyberSecurity #Berlin Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI)  Kim Nguyen Claudia Otto

comments.text: The forensic angle worth adding: once exfiltrated data surfaces on a leak site, the real evidentiary question shifts from 'what was taken' to 'what can be reconstructed and attributed with chain-of-custody integrity' — that distinction matters far more for prosecutors than the TB figure.
Do you see organisations building the 'authority envelope' you describe before or only after an incident forces the conversation — in your experience is procurement of these controls ever proactive?

We see the same gap in ransomware and extortion cases we work on: identity and access logs are usually clean, but nobody can show who authorised the action that followed a legitimate-looking credential use. That gap is where liability disputes actually get decided.

posts.title: Security is everyone's responsibility...
posts.author: Daniel Dib
posts.snippet:
Security is everyone's responsibility...


There was a time, where systems people worked on systems, security people on security, and networking people on networking. Sure, there was some overlap, but security was often bolted on later rather than being taken into consideration into the design phase.

Then, ransomware became a thing and for the first time even management started considering security because being down costs money.

Later, we got laws and regulations that associate a real cost to poor security. Before, worst case you got named and shamed and everyone had forgot after a week or two.

Now, we live in a world where adversaries have better resources than we do. They are more well funded and have better tools because they became early adopters of LLMs.

Like my dear friend, Emanuel Lipschütz always says, don't bring a knife to a gunfight!

Running a pentest once a year is not going to cut it any longer. You need to use tools like AI agents to continuously test your infrastructure and code. If you're not doing it, I can guarantee someone else is, and it's just a matter of time before they find a way.

That's why OpenAI and others are starting to work together to collaboratively develop cyber defense measures. Is this marketing? Yes. Can it still be useful? I hope so.

Has your organization started using these type of tools?

We're regularly brought in after the fact, and the pattern is consistent: technical defence matured, but nobody had mapped who makes the call on paying, reporting or negotiating when the incident actually happens.

Si eres administrador de una empresa y crees que un ciberataque es “un problema del informático”, deberías leer esto.

Porque quizá el verdadero problema empiece después del ciberataque.

Hoy una empresa puede sufrir una interrupción por un ransomware, un fallo de un proveedor tecnológico, un error de software o incluso una mala implementación de Inteligencia Artificial.

Y cuando el negocio se para, aparecen algunas preguntas:

1.- ¿Se habían identificado correctamente los riesgos?

2.- ¿Se habían tomado medidas suficientes para proteger la empresa?

3.- ¿Se gestionó correctamente la crisis?

4.- ¿Puede llegar alguien a cuestionar las decisiones tomadas por los administradores?

La realidad es que el riesgo tecnológico está empezando a escalar directamente hasta la dirección.

Por eso, no solo debemos intentar reducir el impacto de un incidente. También debemos estar preparados para responder, recuperar la actividad y proteger a quienes toman las decisiones.

Un Seguro de Ciberriesgo puede proteger a la empresa frente a las consecuencias de un incidente cibernético.

Un Seguro de Responsabilidad Civil D&O puede proteger a administradores y directivos frente a determinadas reclamaciones derivadas de sus decisiones y actuaciones.

La noticia de SegurosNews pone sobre la mesa algo que, en mi opinión, todos los empresarios deberían plantearse. No se trata únicamente de preguntarnos “¿podemos sufrir un ciberataque?”

La pregunta importante es:

¿Qué consecuencias tendría para mi empresa y para mí como administrador si mañana ocurre?

Porque el riesgo ya no está únicamente en los servidores. También puede estar en las decisiones que tomamos desde el despacho.

Y ahí es donde una buena gestión de riesgos y un buen asesoramiento asegurador pueden marcar la diferencia.

Administradores y empresarios: ¿habéis revisado ya vuestro riesgo cibernético y vuestra protección como dirección?

posts.title: 🛡️ BULLETPROOF HOSTING EXPLAINED
posts.author: Steve M Netscalers
posts.snippet:
🛡️ BULLETPROOF HOSTING EXPLAINED
Bulletproof hosting—BPH—refers to hosting infrastructure operated with unusually permissive policies or deliberate resistance to credible abuse complaints, suspensions and disruption.
Cybercriminals may use these services to keep malicious infrastructure online for longer than it would remain with a responsible hosting provider.
Despite the name, this infrastructure is not genuinely “bulletproof.” It can still be identified, blocked, seized or disrupted.
🔄 SIMPLIFIED INFRASTRUCTURE FLOW
1️⃣ Infrastructure obtained
A threat actor obtains servers, domains or other hosted services.
2️⃣ Malicious services deployed
The infrastructure may support phishing, malware distribution, command-and-control systems, ransomware operations, spam or fraud.
3️⃣ Targets or infected devices connect
Users may be directed to malicious websites, while compromised devices communicate with attacker-controlled systems.
4️⃣ Activity detected and reported
Security researchers, network defenders, service providers or law enforcement identify and report the activity.
5️⃣ Defenders respond
Organisations monitor connections, block confirmed malicious indicators, preserve evidence, report findings and coordinate disruption.
🔍 POSSIBLE DEFENSIVE INDICATORS
⚠️ Repeated association with confirmed malicious activity
⚠️ Persistent abuse despite credible reports
⚠️ Related domains or infrastructure changing frequently
⚠️ Connections to known phishing, malware or command-and-control systems
🛡️ HOW TO REDUCE THE RISK
✅ Use reputable threat intelligence
✅ Monitor DNS, proxy, firewall and endpoint telemetry
✅ Apply email, DNS and web filtering
✅ Restrict unnecessary outbound connections
✅ Investigate suspicious network activity
✅ Keep systems and endpoint protection updated
✅ Follow established incident-response procedures
✅ Report confirmed malicious activity
⚠️ IMPORTANT
An IP address, hosting location or privacy service is not proof of malicious intent. Legitimate infrastructure can also be compromised or abused without the provider’s knowledge.
Defensive decisions should use multiple sources of evidence and consider the possibility of false positives.
💡 IDENTIFY. BLOCK. REPORT. DISRUPT.
🌐 NETSCALERS | TECHNICAL EXPLAINER
#BulletproofHosting #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #NetworkSecurity #IncidentResponse #NetScalers

posts.title: The ATO follows the money. That's really the whole job, when you strip it back.
posts.author: Christine McWilliams
posts.snippet:
The ATO follows the money. That's really the whole job, when you strip it back.

I have a handful of clients whose structures involve companies inside companies. A fund invests in Company A, which loans money to Company B, which might hold the actual asset. 

Individually, most of these smaller companies have no audit requirement of their own. But the moment the fund is investing through them, I need visibility into all of it.

Every loan between those entities has to be on arm's length terms. A genuine interest rate, genuine documentation, nothing that looks like it's there to move money around without a commercial reason behind it.

What I'm actually doing is tracing the path. Money goes in at the top, moves through however many entities sit in between, and lands somewhere at the bottom, a development, a related party, a straightforward investment. My job is to follow that whole chain and confirm it's clean at every step.

For some of my longer-standing clients, we've built actual diagrams to track the structure.

There’s a very clear pattern I've noticed. When the accountant gets ahead of the structure, understands it before it changes, not after, the trustee tends to keep them looped in too.

By the time I'm untangling it, it's already cost someone time and money. Get ahead of the structure, and none of that has to happen.

posts.title: I have seen a claimant obtain an award and still struggle to turn it into money because the respondent had no identifiable assets.
posts.author: Dushyant Krishnan
posts.snippet:
I have seen a claimant obtain an award and still struggle to turn it into money because the respondent had no identifiable assets.

That experience changed the point at which I begin analysing recovery.

Before advising a client to commence arbitration, I ask a few basic questions:

What is the realistic value of the claim?
Not merely the amount demanded, but the amount likely to be awarded after accounting for evidentiary gaps, possible defences, interest and costs.

What can the award be enforced against?
The client’s own records and lawful public searches are useful starting points for identifying bank accounts, receivables, property, investments and deposits. Ownership and existing encumbrances matter as much as the existence of an asset.

Is the respondent still commercially viable?
An operating business with continuing revenue presents different recovery prospects from a defunct company. But ongoing operations alone do not establish an ability to pay: existing debt, secured creditors and insolvency concerns also matter.

Can assets be preserved?
Where the facts justify interim protection, preserving an identifiable asset may materially improve recovery prospects. A vague belief that the respondent “must have assets somewhere” is not enough.

What is the all-in cost?
The relevant figure includes tribunal fees, legal costs, interim proceedings, enforcement and, where necessary, asset tracing across jurisdictions.

The outcome need not always be binary.

A strong claim against an operational respondent with a credible capacity to pay may be worth pursuing, even if specific assets have not yet been identified.

An uncertain asset position may favour a discounted settlement or a tightly budgeted arbitration, with spending reassessed as more information becomes available.

It is probably better to write off a claim against a defunct shell, with no assets, cash flows or independently liable guarantor.

The question is not simply whether the claimant can win. It is whether the likely recovery justifies the cost of getting there.

Part 16 of Understanding Mid-Caps. Today, two S&P 400 ETFs, and whether cheaper is the better pick.

So when would you pick the more expensive IJH?
For liquidity and options. IJH is one of the larger and more heavily traded mid-cap ETFs by assets and volume, with a deep options market and tight bid-ask spreads. The bid-ask spread is the small gap between the buy price and the sell price. A tighter spread means you lose less when you trade. 

For a long-term holder making occasional trades, this difference is small. For someone trading large size, or writing options against the position, IJH's deeper market can matter more than the 0.02% fee difference.

The nuance. A 0.02% fee gap is small in absolute terms. If IJH's tighter spreads or options depth save an active trader more than that, the pricier fund can be the better net choice for that investor. For everyone else, the cheaper SPMD is the simpler answer.

🚨 Alerte arnaque: faux courrier des impôts sur les cryptos. Attention ⚠️

J’ai reçu un courrier présenté comme une « mise en demeure » de la DGFiP concernant la directive DAC8 et les actifs numériques.

Logo officiel, vocabulaire juridique, menace d’amende, délai très court et QR code à scanner pour s’inscrire sur un prétendu portail: 

tout est conçu pour provoquer la peur comme ceux de l'administration fiscale et récupérer des informations sensibles.

C’est une arnaque.

J’ai masqué mon adresse sur la copie publiée ici, mais elle apparaît bien sur le courrier reçu, avec mon identité. Ce n’est donc pas un simple spam anonyme: 

c’est un courrier ciblé, envoyé à domicile, suffisamment crédible pour piéger et effrayer beaucoup de monde.

Dans le contexte des accès illégitimes et du vol de données récemment reconnus par la DGFiP, cette situation est particulièrement révoltante. L’administration indique que les espaces particuliers n’ont pas été compromis, mais des données fiscales et personnelles ont pu être exposées lors de l’incident.

Quand des fraudeurs disposent d’une identité, d’une adresse et d’éléments permettant de faire croire à un dossier fiscal réel, les risques ne se limitent pas au phishing: 

usurpation d’identité, extorsion, harcèlement, cambriolage ciblé ou pression sur les détenteurs présumés de crypto-actifs.

❌ Ne scannez pas le QR code.  
❌ Ne connectez aucun compte crypto.  
❌ Ne communiquez jamais vos identifiants, clés privées ou phrase de récupération.  

✅ Vérifiez uniquement depuis votre espace particulier sur impots.gouv.fr, saisi manuellement dans votre navigateur.

La cybersécurité des données fiscales n’est pas un détail technique: 

elle concerne directement la sécurité des citoyens.

posts.title: Des « experts cyber », on en entend beaucoup ces derniers temps.
posts.author: Cyril PINEAU
posts.snippet:
Des « experts cyber », on en entend beaucoup ces derniers temps.
Certains sont crédibles, probablement. Mais ce terme me dérange, car je ne sais jamais ce qu'il y a derrière.

La cyber n'est pas un métier. C'est une famille de métiers qui n'ont presque rien en commun, un peu comme dans la sécurité routière.

➡️ Les spécialistes de l'offensif, du pentest : les crash-tests. Ils cassent pour savoir ce qui tiendra le jour de l'accident.
➡️ Les spécialistes du défensif, le SOC : les gendarmes et leurs radars. Ils surveillent, dissuadent, analysent, interceptent avant l'impact.
➡️ La GRC, la gouvernance : la prévention routière. Ils aménagent les carrefours dangereux, définissent les règles, font passer les messages de prévention. Souvent perçus comme des rabat-joie (mon quotidien).
➡️ La réponse à incident, le CSIRT : les pompiers. Ils arrivent après l'accident, prennent en charge les blessés, évitent le sur-accident.
➡️ Le forensic : les enquêteurs. Ils établissent les causes, les circonstances, et parfois les responsabilités.
➡️ L'OSINT : le renseignement. Ceux qui connaissent la route avant d'y rouler : les points noirs, les habitudes, les angles morts.

Et j'en oublie : la crypto, la sécurité produit, l'embarqué, l'IAM…

Personne n'est expert en tout cela. Il faudrait avoir vécu cinq vies en vingt ans.

Alors quand on me présente un « expert cyber », j'ai toujours du mal à comprendre sur quel périmètre exact il est expert.

posts.title: At the end of last year, a rumor spread fast through the Chinese Web3 community: police in cities like Hangzhou and Chengdu were allegedly stopping people on the street or knocking
posts.author: Honglin Liu
posts.snippet:
At the end of last year, a rumor spread fast through the Chinese Web3 community: police in cities like Hangzhou and Chengdu were allegedly stopping people on the street or knocking on doors, and if a crypto app or wallet assets were found on the phone, demanding an "immediate transfer." Many practitioners were genuinely shaken. After cross-checking with multiple sources, our criminal defense team concluded this is very likely a rumor blown out of proportion — a self-media tactic, not a real policy.

Instead of feeding the fear, we broke it down with legal reasoning. Why doesn't "confiscate on sight" hold up in law? Two basics: street interrogation power is not arbitrary search power — unlocking a phone to inspect private apps without a search warrant is procedurally unlawful; and disposing of seized assets follows an extremely strict process — forcing a transfer without a case filing or seizure order could expose the officers themselves to charges like abuse of power or even extortion. Regulation is tightening, yes, but such overreach can never be the norm. If the extreme case ever happens: verify identity, no transfer without paperwork, only to official accounts, appeal afterwards. Fear comes from the unknown; safety comes from professionalism.

posts.title: The line between ethical security research and financial extortion is blurring in the crypto industry.
posts.author: Giancarlo Perlas
posts.snippet:
The line between ethical security research and financial extortion is blurring in the crypto industry.

After a massive exploit targeting the Liquid Network that compromised 4,000 Bitcoin, the self-proclaimed white-hat hackers returned 85% of the stolen assets to Blockstream while keeping 598.5 BTC.

Valued at roughly $47 million, this exorbitant bounty has sparked fierce backlash in the cryptocurrency community because of its scale and the forceful tactics used.

While white-hat bounties are standard practice designed to incentivize security researchers, industry benchmarks typically cap these rewards around $10 million or roughly 5% to 10% of the recovered funds.

In this case, the group unilaterally set a 15% bug bounty and communicated largely via Bitcoin OP_RETURN messages rather than engaging in traditional direct negotiations.

Furthermore, the researchers refused to return any funds until Blockstream proved it had successfully patched the underlying vulnerability.

The unprecedented approach leaves significant collateral damage in its wake.

Retaining such a substantial amount could create a deficit in the Liquid Network reserve backing, directly threatening Liquid Bitcoin's 1:1 peg to native Bitcoin.

As discussions around potential legal action heat up, the outcome of this dispute could set a dangerous precedent for future security disclosures and the delicate relationship between protocols and independent security researchers.

posts.title: Plant the key. Walk away. Wait for the moment that matters.
posts.author: Brian C.
posts.snippet:
Plant the key. Walk away. Wait for the moment that matters.

“Deploy now, exploit later” is the quiet operator in modern cyber conflict. It is the actor who seeds code, credentials, misconfigurations, or dormant access long before anyone notices. Sometimes it is a criminal group. Sometimes it is a state unit. Sometimes it is a contractor working under direction. The identity shifts. The pattern does not.

#What: A strategy built on patience. Instead of smashing the door today, the attacker slips a key under the mat and leaves. The goal is future leverage: data theft, paralysis, extortion, or geopolitical pressure. The defining feature is delayed activation.

#Where: Inside cloud tenants, identity providers, CI/CD pipelines, firmware, unmanaged SaaS, forgotten servers, and third‑party integrations. They hide where organisations rarely audit and survive migrations, staff turnover, and vendor churn.

#Why: Because timing is power. Waiting lets the attacker strike when defenders are distracted, under pressure, or politically exposed and accumulate layered footholds that are hard to unwind.

#When: Deployment happens during routine operations: a normal patch cycle, a rushed rollout, a contractor engagement, a supply‑chain update. Exploitation comes months or years later, when logs are gone and memories have faded.

#How: Insert something small. Ensure it blends in. Leave it dormant. Monitor from afar. Activate only when conditions favour maximum impact. Defenders counter by treating every deployment as a potential future risk: strict provenance checks, continuous validation, and aggressive removal of legacy access paths.

#PQC angle: The same patience applies to cryptographic risk. Adversaries can harvest today and decrypt later once quantum arrives. Treat every long‑lived secret, every dormant integration, and every unmanaged key as a future liability. Build crypto agility now, rotate to quantum‑safe algorithms on a schedule, and remove legacy access paths before they become tomorrow’s breach.

posts.title: Liquid BTC (the Liquid Network) is accusing "white-hack hackers" of stealing $320 million of Bitcoin from the Liquid Federation wallet "via the SideSwap PAK (Peg-out Authorization
posts.author: Evan Kohlmann
posts.snippet:
Liquid BTC (the Liquid Network) is accusing "white-hack hackers" of stealing $320 million of Bitcoin from the Liquid Federation wallet "via the SideSwap PAK (Peg-out Authorization Key)."  Liquid is nonetheless insisting that the key "was not compromised" and that deposits and withdrawals of LBTC deposits have been frozen at major crypto exchanges--as well as freezing bridge notes "so no new transactions can be submitted to the network."  

According to Liquid, their sidechain has been "effectively... paused" until the issue is resolved--and they claim that they have attempted to contact the hackers on-chain with a signed message.  

It's also not entirely clear why Liquid believes the perpetrators were specifically "white-hack" hackers, or how likely it is for the money to be returned.  So-called white hacks typically target systems in order to surface critical security vulnerabilities *before* malicious actors can gain access, not to steal $320 million worth of crypto.  It's possible that, in this case, the perpetrators are seeking some kind of bug bounty before returning the stolen funds, but that would still amount to criminal extortion.

(Source links in the comments)
posts.reason: A detailed breakdown of the Liquid Bridge theft, the extortion question, and regulatory freeze response that directly interests lawyers, compliance officers, and law enforcement investigating crypto financial crime and recovery.

comments.text: The insistence that the peg-out authorization key was 'not compromised' while $320 million moved out through it is the detail worth scrutinizing - either the key's authorization logic itself was flawed, or there's an access path Liquid hasn't disclosed yet, and that distinction matters for how exchanges assess counterparty risk going forward.
Has Liquid indicated whether the signed on-chain message to the attackers included any concrete terms, or is it still just an open contact attempt with no negotiation framework?

Freezing deposits and withdrawals across major exchanges is the right first move and mirrors what we typically push for immediately after an incident like this - the choke-point at centralized exchanges is often the only leverage available before funds get layered through swaps and bridges.
